title: Episode 135: Franklin Pierce and Bleeding Kansas: The Tragic President
description:
In November eighteen fifty-two, forty-seven-year-old Franklin Pierce of New Hampshire won one of the most lopsided electoral landslides in American history, carrying twenty-seven of thirty-one states. Dashing, handsome, and charming, Pierce was hailed as a young unifier who would put the bitter sectional controversies over slavery to rest forever.

Yet two months before his inauguration, unspeakable personal tragedy struck. While traveling by train from Boston to Concord, the presidential passenger car derailed and tumbled down an embankment. Pierce and his wife Jane watched in horror as their only surviving child, eleven-year-old Benny, was crushed to death before their eyes. Entering the White House emotionally broken and wracked by survivor's guilt, Pierce governed under a cloud of bottomless grief, while his traumatized wife locked herself in darkened upstairs rooms writing letters of apology to her dead child.

Desperate to maintain party unity, Pierce yielded to Illinois Senator Stephen A. Douglas, signing the disastrous Kansas-Nebraska Act of eighteen fifty-four. By repealing the sacred Missouri Compromise and leaving the expansion of slavery to 'popular sovereignty,' Pierce ignited a localized civil war in the prairie territories: 'Bleeding Kansas.' Pro-slavery 'Border Ruffians' battled anti-slavery Free-Staters, John Brown launched the midnight Pottawatomie massacre, and Senator Charles Sumner was beaten senseless with a heavy cane on the floor of the United States Senate. Here is George with the heartbreaking story of the most tragic presidency in American history.

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. Today, we step into the troubled presidency of our fourteenth chief executive, Franklin Pierce. Pierce entered the presidency with high hopes of national unity, but arrived at the White House a broken, grieving father following the horrific death of his son. Paralyzed by sorrow and manipulated by ambitious politicians, Pierce signed legislation that tore the country apart, unleashing the bloodbath of Bleeding Kansas and setting America on an irreversible course toward civil war. Here is George with the tragic story.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: THE LANDSLIDE AND THE DERAILMENT
In November eighteen fifty-two, Franklin Pierce of New Hampshire appeared to be the luckiest man on the American continent. A handsome, charismatic Mexican-American War veteran and former senator, Pierce was the ultimate compromise candidate—a 'doughface,' a Northern man with Southern principles. In the presidential election, Pierce obliterated Whig candidate Winfield Scott, winning two hundred and fifty-four electoral votes to Scott's forty-two. At age forty-eight, he was the youngest man ever elected President up to that time.
Then, in a single horrific instant, his life was shattered. On January sixth, eighteen fifty-three, two months before the inauguration, Pierce, his wife Jane, and their beloved eleven-year-old son Benny were traveling by train from Andover, Massachusetts, to Concord, New Hampshire. A few miles outside Andover, a broken wheel axle fractured, and the passenger coach broke loose, hurtling off the tracks and plunging down a steep rocky embankment.
Franklin and Jane were bruised, but when Pierce reached for his son, he was confronted with an image of unspeakable horror. Benny had been thrown forward and nearly decapitated by the splintered timbers of the train carriage, killed instantly before his parents' eyes. Pierce desperately threw his wool coat over the boy's body to shield his wife from the sight, but Jane had already seen it. The First Lady collapsed in hysterical agony. She became convinced that God had demanded the life of their only remaining child as a sacrifice so that Franklin would be unburdened by family love and could focus entirely on governing the country.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: THE SHADOW IN THE EXECUTIVE MANSION
On March fourth, eighteen fifty-three, Franklin Pierce stood on the Capitol portico to take the oath of office. A wet, freezing snow fell upon his bare head. Out of deep religious doubt following Benny's death, Pierce refused to place his hand on a Bible to 'swear' the oath, choosing instead to 'affirm' it on a law book. He delivered his entire three-thousand-word inaugural address completely from memory without notes, an impressive feat of oratory, but his heart was dead within him.
The White House became a somber, weeping mausoleum. First Lady Jane Pierce draped the mansion's mirrors, chandeliers, and furniture in black crepe. She refused to attend the inaugural ball, did not host social functions, and spent her days secluded in a darkened second-floor bedroom, reading the Bible and writing heart-wrenching letters addressed to her dead son Benny, begging him to forgive his father's political ambitions.
Franklin Pierce, wracked with unendurable grief and survivor's guilt, was emotionally adrift. He suffered from severe insomnia, wandering the silent corridors of the White House late at night, and began drinking heavily to numb his pain. Lacking the emotional stamina to enforce his own will, Pierce became dangerously dependent on dominant, aggressive politicians who possessed their own fierce ideological agendas—most notably his Secretary of War, Jefferson Davis of Mississippi, and the charismatic powerhouse of the Senate, Stephen A. Douglas of Illinois.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: STEPHEN DOUGLAS AND THE NEBRASKA GAMBLE
In early eighteen fifty-four, Senator Stephen A. Douglas approached President Pierce with an audacious, fateful legislative proposal. Douglas, known as the 'Little Giant,' was an ambitious Western expansionist determined to build a transcontinental railroad connecting Chicago to the Pacific coast. To make the northern route viable, Douglas needed to organize the vast, unorganized prairie wilderness west of Iowa and Missouri into formal federal territories.
However, Southern senators, led by David Rice Atchison of Missouri, blocked the bill. Under the sacred Missouri Compromise of eighteen twenty, all territory in the Louisiana Purchase north of latitude thirty-six degrees, thirty minutes was permanently closed to slavery. Southern leaders refused to create new territories that would inevitably become free states, surrounding the slave state of Missouri with free soil.
Douglas devised a high-stakes, fatal gamble. He proposed dividing the region into two territories—Kansas and Nebraska—and repealing the Missouri Compromise line entirely. Instead of federal prohibition, the question of slavery would be decided by 'popular sovereignty'—allowing the settlers who moved into the territory to vote on whether to allow human bondage. On Sunday, January twenty-second, eighteen fifty-four, Douglas and Jefferson Davis visited the White House, cornering a weary Franklin Pierce and convincing him that the bill was essential for Democratic Party unity. Pierce agreed to throw the full weight of the presidency behind it.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: THE KANSAS-NEBRASKA SHOCKWAVE
When the Kansas-Nebraska Act was introduced in Congress, it detonated an explosive moral earthquake across the North. To millions of Northern citizens, the Missouri Compromise of eighteen twenty was not an ordinary statute; it was a sacred, unbreakable covenant forged by the founding generation to restrict the spread of slavery. Repealing it was seen as an act of monstrous betrayal by the 'Slave Power.'
Protest meetings erupted in every Northern town. Church bells tolled in mourning, and Douglas joked that he could travel from Boston to Chicago by the light of his own burning effigies. Despite intense opposition, Pierce used the iron hammer of executive patronage—threatening to strip federal jobs from any Democrat who voted against the bill—to force it through Congress. On May thirtieth, eighteen fifty-four, Pierce signed the Kansas-Nebraska Act into law.
The political fallout was catastrophic. The Whig Party, unable to bridge the divide between Northern and Southern members, shattered into pieces and collapsed permanently. In small schoolhouses in Ripon, Wisconsin, and Jackson, Michigan, anti-slavery Whigs, Free Soilers, and anti-Nebraska Democrats banded together to form a brand-new political movement dedicated to stopping the expansion of slavery into Western territories: the Republican Party. And on the windswept prairies of Kansas, popular sovereignty transformed democracy into a killing ground.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: BORDER RUFFIANS AND THE SACK OF LAWRENCE
By making the expansion of slavery dependent on who arrived first, the Kansas-Nebraska Act turned Kansas into a deadly territorial race. In New England, wealthy abolitionists formed the New England Emigrant Aid Company, funding thousands of Free-State settlers to move to Kansas, arming them with the latest Sharps breech-loading rifles, which became famously known as 'Beecher's Bibles' after the fiery abolitionist preacher Henry Ward Beecher.
Across the border in Missouri, pro-slavery forces mobilized in fury. Thousands of heavily armed Missourians, known as 'Border Ruffians,' rode across the border on election days. Brandishing revolvers, bowie knives, and whiskey jugs, they drove election judges from polling places, stuffed ballot boxes with thousands of fraudulent votes, and elected an illegitimate, radical pro-slavery territorial legislature at Lecompton.
Free-State settlers refused to recognize the bogus government, establishing their own rival free-state capital at Topeka. Kansas had two governments, two constitutions, and two armed militias staring each other down. President Pierce made a disastrous, partisan choice: he officially recognized the fraudulent pro-slavery legislature and denounced the Free-State government as treasonous rebels.
On May twenty-first, eighteen fifty-six, an army of eight hundred pro-slavery Border Ruffians under Douglas County Sheriff Samuel Jones marched into the anti-slavery stronghold of Lawrence, Kansas. Flying banners reading 'Southern Rights,' they shelled and burned the Free State Hotel, smashed the printing presses of two abolitionist newspapers and threw the type into the Kansas River, and looted private homes in the infamous Sack of Lawrence.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: BLOOD IN THE SENATE AND POTTAWATOMIE CREEK
The violence in Kansas detonated on the floor of the United States Capitol itself. On May nineteenth and twentieth, eighteen fifty-six, Senator Charles Sumner of Massachusetts delivered a blistering, two-day oration titled 'The Crime Against Kansas.' Sumner viciously insulted South Carolina Senator Andrew Butler, comparing Butler's devotion to slavery to a knight who had chosen 'a mistress who, though ugly to others, is always lovely to him; I mean the harlot, slavery.'
Two days later, on May twenty-second, Butler's nephew, South Carolina Representative Preston Brooks, walked into the nearly empty Senate chamber. Approaching Sumner seated at his heavy mahogany desk, Brooks shouted that Sumner had libeled his state and kin, and proceeded to strike Sumner over the head with a heavy, gold-headed gutta-percha walking cane with savage fury. Trapped beneath his bolted desk, Sumner ripped the heavy desk from the floorboards in agony before collapsing unconscious in a pool of his own blood. Brooks struck him dozens of times until the cane shattered. Southern admirers mailed Brooks hundreds of new canes inscribed 'Hit him again!' while the North was galvanized in horror.
Two days after the caning of Sumner, news of the assault and the sack of Lawrence reached an abolitionist zealot living in a cabin near Osawatomie, Kansas: fifty-six-year-old John Brown. Believing he was God's chosen instrument of divine vengeance, Brown led four of his sons and three companions along Pottawatomie Creek on the night of May twenty-fourth. Dragging five pro-slavery settlers from their cabins, Brown's men hacked them to death with heavy broadswords. The civil war had officially begun in Kansas.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: CAST OUT BY HIS OWN PARTY
By the summer of eighteen fifty-six, more than two hundred men had been murdered in guerrilla warfare across 'Bleeding Kansas.' Crops were burned, homes were looted, and peaceful settlers walked their plows with cocked rifles strapped to their shoulders. Franklin Pierce's administration was in smoking ruins. The man who had been elected in an overwhelming landslide as the great unifier had become the most despised president in American history.
When the Democratic National Convention met in Cincinnati in June eighteen fifty-six, Franklin Pierce desperately sought renomination to vindicate his record. But Democratic delegates recognized that Pierce was a political corpse. In an unprecedented, humiliating rebuke, the party discarded its own sitting President on the seventeenth ballot, nominating James Buchanan of Pennsylvania—a man who had been safely out of the country serving as minister to Great Britain and was completely untainted by the blood of Kansas.
Franklin Pierce remains the only elected President of the United States to actively seek re-election and be denied nomination by his own political party.
Upon leaving office in March eighteen fifty-seven, a reporter asked Pierce what he intended to do next. Pierce gave a weary, bitter, tragic reply: 'There is nothing left to do but to get drunk.' He returned to New Hampshire, an outcast reviled by his neighbors, drinking heavily until his death from cirrhosis in eighteen sixty-nine.
Franklin Pierce was not a wicked man; he was an ordinary, grief-stricken man crushed beneath an extraordinary, unforgiving historical crisis. His presidency stands as an enduring, haunting warning: that in moments of great moral confrontation, compromise with injustice only breeds greater catastrophe.

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
Franklin Pierce's signing of the Kansas-Nebraska Act ignited the prairie fires of civil war and fractured the American political system forever. Next week, we turn to the second chapter of Franklin Pierce's presidency: his aggressive expansionist dreams in the Gadsden Purchase and the scandalous secret Ostend Manifesto—a plot to wrest the island of Cuba from Spain by force of arms to create an American Caribbean empire. Until then, thank you for listening to Most Fascinating Stories.
